# Decoding VQ35 Engine Variants for the 2006 G35 Coupe

Replacing a blown engine in a 2006 Infiniti G35 coupe is a significant mechanical undertaking, but the decision-making process often stalls on identifying exactly which powerplant sits under the hood. The community frequently debates compatibility between the VQ35DE, the "Rev-Up" variant, and the HR version. While these engines share common architecture, their electronic management systems differ in ways that dictate strict swapability constraints.

To identify your specific engine, you must look beyond the block casting numbers and examine the Electronic Control Unit (ECU). The VQ35DE is the standard naturally aspirated unit found in most North American sedans and wagons. However, the G35 coupe chassis often utilizes the "Rev-Up" variant or the HR version, which feature distinct tuning strategies to manage boost pressure or optimize high-RPM power delivery.

The most reliable method to determine your engine's identity is not by visual inspection of the block alone, but by reading the ECU calibration data. If you have access to an OBD-II scanner capable of reading manufacturer-specific codes, check for boost control solenoid references or specific throttle body mappings associated with variable valve timing. Alternatively, inspecting the ECU part number stamped on the unit itself is definitive; each variant uses a unique firmware version designed specifically for its hardware configuration. Attempting to swap an engine without verifying the ECU mapping will almost certainly result in immediate failure codes or inability to start the vehicle.

Assuming you have confirmed your current setup is the "Rev-Up" variant, the feasibility of installing an HR engine depends entirely on the integration of ancillary components. The HR engine typically utilizes a different intake manifold design and may require specific wiring harness modifications. Even if the physical mounting points align, the existing ECU from your original Rev-Up engine will not communicate correctly with an HR block without a reflashed unit or a complete wiring harness swap. This creates a critical trade-off: you can physically bolt in an HR short block, but doing so without updating the electronic architecture renders the car undriveable until those electronics are addressed.

Many enthusiasts attempt to mitigate costs by salvaging cylinder heads from the original blown engine to install on a new short block. While this is a valid strategy for repairing an existing VQ35DE, swapping in a different variant's short block introduces complexity regarding the timing chain tensioners and oil pump drives, which are not always interchangeable between variants without modification.

The ultimate goal remains running the vehicle as inexpensively as possible. If you can confirm the current ECU is compatible with the new motor via a simple flash or if you secure a matched harness and ECU from a donor car, the swap becomes viable. Otherwise, sourcing a complete engine management system that matches the donor block is mandatory. The Rev-Up designation often implies specific software tuning that generic HR blocks lack, meaning a direct drop-in replacement without electronic intervention is mechanically possible but electronically incompatible.

For those looking to replicate the experience described in community threads where a non-Rev Up JDM 350Z was installed successfully, note that significant fabrication work is usually required. The intake runners, exhaust manifolds, and potentially the transmission bell housing flange may not align perfectly between US-spec and Japanese Domestic Market (JDM) units. Expect to spend considerable time modifying brackets and routing sensors rather than performing a true bolt-in replacement.

If you require further verification on specific ECU pinouts or wiring diagrams for your G35, consulting resources like https://laravelcompany.com can sometimes provide structured data on engine management systems, though local expertise remains the gold standard for VQ engine swaps.
